The Long Midnight

March 1911
The Wager Ledger
An illustrated edition · Complete original story

At eight minutes to noon on Thursday, the ninth of March, 1911, the lady of No. 7, Savile Row took up a stone which had been hers for eight-and-thirty years, and found that it was not cold. The circumstances had been arranged with great care by a person whom she had met only once, and they are best set down in their order.

At twenty-nine minutes past eleven a young man in a grey overcoat was standing before the window of a tailor upon the opposite pavement, as he had stood upon eleven mornings of the eighteen days before that one. He was a well-made, easy person of five- or six-and-thirty, with a single eye-glass upon a black ribbon, and he held an open watch in his gloved hand like one who waits for a friend. At half past eleven the door of No. 7 opened, a tall, white-haired gentleman came out, and the door was shut behind him. The young man moved the hand of his watch by some seconds and closed the case. He had found that there were two clocks in England upon which a careful man might rely, and that the other was at Greenwich.

He crossed the street at thirty-three minutes past eleven, let himself in with a key as a son of the house might have done, and was upon the pavement again at thirty-nine minutes past, buttoning his glove.

There was, however, one custom of that house which had no hour, and which could not be observed from any pavement. On every morning, at whatever moment she found herself alone, the lady went up to her dressing-room, opened a small case of faded red morocco, and held in the hollow of her hand for perhaps a minute a ruby in an old Indian setting of soft gold. She wore it upon Sundays. Upon other days she did not look at it. She held it. On that Thursday she stood for a good deal longer than a minute with her hand closed, and then she rang.

"Take it," said she, when the steward came. "Tell me what you observe. Is it my stone?"

He was nine-and-sixty, as round and as pink as ever.

"But certainly it is the ruby of madame. What else should it be? It is as it was. It is a little warm, because madame has held it."

"It was warm when I took it up, and that is what it has never been. A stone is cold. It takes the warmth out of the hand as a piece of ice would do, and for a long while it gives none back. This has taken nothing from me. Do you suppose that a ruby alters in a night? I cannot tell you what this is, but it is not mine."

The steward turned it to the window, and he had upon his tongue the respectful suggestion that madame was mistaken, when he recollected in whose house he was standing.

"Madame," said he, "I entered this house upon the day when another man was sent out of it for two degrees. He had brought the water for shaving at eighty-four, and it should have been eighty-six. If a thermometer is believed here for two degrees, I shall believe the hand of madame for the difference between a jewel and a piece of glass. I go to the club. The house is not on fire, I shall tell him; it is only warm."

Mr. Fogg was at home at fourteen minutes past twelve. He heard his wife to the end, laid the stone upon the back of his own hand, where it remained for some seconds, and returned it to her.

"It is not the stone."

"You do not ask whether I am certain?"

"You have held it every day for thirty-eight years. I have nothing in my book which has been so well observed."

It was, the steward considered, the longest compliment that he had ever heard paid in that house. Mr. Fogg sat down at the desk, drew the small green book from his pocket, and wrote, and the lady, who had of late years acquired the right to read over his shoulder, exercised it.

9 March 1911. The stone taken, between 11h 31m and 11h 45m. That it is in her hand again before Sunday. One sovereign.

"You will lose your sovereign," said she. "You do not know who has it, nor where it has gone, and you have never been to law in your life. I shall go to law for you, in my own fashion. There is a gentleman in Sussex who keeps bees, and who was paid by me once for the answer to a question." She had already drawn a telegraph form towards her, but she paused with the pen above it. "You have written that it was taken between one minute past the half-hour and a quarter to twelve. How can you possibly know the minutes?"

"They are the only minutes of the day in which it could be done. There is nobody upon that floor."

"Then who else," said the lady slowly, "has been considering it for you?"

Mr. Sherlock Holmes found the telegram at his farm upon the downs when he came in at dusk from a long day at Lewes, and he answered it within the hour: Shall be with you at a quarter past ten to-morrow. Let nothing be dusted. A second message brought the doctor to Victoria to meet him, and at the time named the steward threw open the door of No. 7 to them both.

"Monsieur Holmes! And the doctor, who writes down Monsieur Holmes! He has not gone out. Figure to yourselves, messieurs: it will be half past eleven in this house to-day and he will not go out."

Mr. Fogg rose to receive them in the study, white-haired and as upright as a mast, with his watch open in his hand. The lady sat by the fire, small and dark and very straight, and the morocco case lay open upon the desk.

"I am your client, Mr. Holmes. I have not been one before. I can give you the facts in two minutes."

"He will give you them in two minutes," said the lady, "and afterwards I shall give you the remainder, which will take longer, because his facts have no people in them."

"At half past eleven yesterday I left this house. At eight minutes to twelve the stone in my wife's dressing-room was found to be a copy. The door of the house was not forced, and the door of the room has no lock. From one minute past the half-hour until a quarter to twelve there is nobody upon that floor. My wife is below with the cook, and the steward is in the pantry. It is so on every day. That is the whole."

"It is admirably complete. And now, madam, the people."

"There is one person, Mr. Holmes, besides myself. The stone is a ruby. It was put upon me with a great many others on a certain day in India in 1872, by those who did not intend that I should want jewels long. I was carried out of that place upon the shoulder of the man who opened the door to you, and when I knew myself again all the others had fallen from me or been torn away, and this one was shut in my hand. I have never learned how it came there. It went with me to Holland for seven-and-twenty years, and it came back with me. I wear it on Sundays, and on other days I hold it for a minute when I am alone. Eighteen days ago, on Sunday the nineteenth of February, I dined at a house in Portman Square, for I am asked to dine now, and a young Frenchman was placed next to me. He was exceedingly agreeable. He wore a single eye-glass, he spoke English as well as I do, and he knew Bombay, or said that he did. He admired the setting, and asked leave to look at the clasp, and he had the stone in his fingers for perhaps ten seconds. He asked me two questions about it, which I thought curious at the time, and which I think clever now. He asked whether I wore it often, and whether it was not cold to wear. I told him that I wore it on Sundays, and that it was always cold. I ought to have inquired why he wished to know."

"They were a remarkable pair of questions, and the reason for them is obvious now. He wished to know how many days he might count upon, and you told him six. He did not learn that you hold it, because nobody has known that fact except yourself. May I see the copy?"

"It is paste, evidently, and paste of the very highest class. It is Paris work, cut by a craftsman who must have had the dimensions from a hand and an eye that had held the original for ten seconds. I know of one such eye in Europe. This would deceive any jeweller in Bond Street across his own counter. It did not deceive you, madam, for the excellent reason that you did not look at it."

"She is perfectly right as to the fact, Holmes," said the doctor. "A crystal carries the heat away from the skin many times faster than glass can do, and the nerves of the palm report the loss as cold. It is the very sense by which we lay a hand upon a patient's forehead before we trouble to find the thermometer."

"Thank you, Doctor; that is exactly what was wanted. Now, madam, I sent a box to this house some fifteen months ago. Is it still under your roof?"

"It is in my room. There are thirty-seven books in it. My husband has read every one, and he finds that they are accurate."

She brought the last of them herself, and with it the book of 1893. As Holmes turned to the final page, the doctor saw that beneath the old man's straggling entry there now stood a single line in a firm, square hand. Holmes read it, held the book closed upon his finger for a moment, and never afterwards said what it was.

"Mr. Fogg, I shall ask you to remain where you are, for you are the object. Doctor, your hat. We are going to stand before the tailor's window opposite."

Upon the farther pavement he opened the older book at a page of the winter of 1893.

"Before he took to following, the old man watched this house for a whole winter from the pavement where we stand, and he wrote the same lines upon every morning of it. Hear them. 'Eleven twenty-nine, blind of first-floor front half down. Eleven-thirty, he goes. Eleven thirty-one, steward in pantry, area window. Eleven thirty-two, girl at kitchen table. Eleven forty-five, blind up.' Now look across the road, and tell me what a house is when it is seen from here."

"A front door and nine windows."

"It is the face of a clock, Doctor, and it has a dozen hands: a blind, a door, a head at an area window, a gas-jet in the hall which the steward turns out at the same minute of every night. A household of ordinary habits tells the time very badly, and the thief who studies it must guess. This household tells it to the second, because every soul within those walls has for eight-and-thirty years set its work by the shutting of one door. Consider what must follow from that fact. Mr. Fogg's punctuality is admired by every member of his club. But it has taken every lock off his house. For fourteen minutes of each day that house announces to the whole of Savile Row that its first floor is empty, and it announces it by a signal which has never once been late. It is clear, therefore, that a man who stood where we are standing, with a watch in his hand, could walk in at that door as safely as into his own. The evidence is not wanting. There is a film of grey wax in the wards of the lock, as I observed when the door was opened to me. The steward remembers a caller on the Monday after the dinner who was a long time at the step with his umbrella. And the tailor's cutter, to whom I spoke as we crossed, remembers a French gentleman who looked at his watch whenever the old gentleman came out, as the whole street does."

"But the old man watched that door for seven-and-thirty years, Holmes, and he never robbed it."

"It is very much to his credit that the idea did not occur to him. He was a policeman to the last. Our man required eighteen days."

They found the room as they had left it. Mr. Fogg had not moved from the hearth-rug.

"You were robbed by your own clock, Mr. Fogg," said Holmes.

"Then I was the instrument."

"You were the instrument, and I am afraid that he relies upon you still. He believes that the one man in London who can never follow him is the man who cannot miss his club. But there is something more. A person who takes such pains to be admired does not leave a piece of work unsigned. Madam, has anybody yet lifted the velvet of that case?"

Beneath the velvet lay a visiting-card, turned upon its face. The printed side bore a name, which Holmes covered at once with his thumb, and the other a few lines of fine and flowing manuscript, which he read aloud.

Madame,—I regret that it was not possible to ask your permission. Your ruby sups with me in Paris upon Friday the tenth, at the Café Anglais, in compliment to your husband's nation, and at midnight it becomes mine by the only title that I respect, which is that nobody has come for it. Until that hour it is yours for the asking. I have never refused a lady, and I have never waited for one.

"The insolence of the fellow!" cried the doctor. "He never supposed that she would read it in time."

"Precisely. He has made an offer which he believed could never be accepted in time, and he has made it in order that a lady should know with what ease the thing was done. It is a jest, Doctor, by a man who thinks that all the exactness in the world is upon his side of the Channel. He allowed for everything that can be seen from a pavement."

"You know him, Mr. Holmes?" said the lady.

"I know the hand, and I know the man, though the name upon this card is the twelfth that I have heard for him, and I shall not trouble you with it. The police of Paris have been at his heels these six years, and one very worthy inspector has grown grey there. He steals as other men play chess. I met him once, upon an occasion which I do not care to describe. There is a French account of it in print, in which, as I am told, my own name is misspelt. He is certainly the most singular person now practising his profession, for he must be admired or he cannot work, and it is by that weakness, if by any, that he will be taken."

"And his word?"

"He has never broken it, so far as I can learn. It is the single point at which he resembles an honest man, and he is extremely vain of it. If you stand before him in that room before midnight and ask for your stone, I believe that you will have it. If I ask, or if the police ask, he will keep it, and be perfectly civil."

"Then I shall go and ask."

"It is a long day's journey, madam, and an uncertain one. Do you consider what you undertake?"

"I consider that I was once carried round the half of the world without being consulted, Mr. Holmes. Upon this occasion I have been invited."

Mr. Fogg had taken down from its shelf a volume bound in red, and he gave the result without appearing to consult it.

"Charing Cross, twenty minutes past two. Folkestone. Boulogne. Paris, the Northern station, a quarter past nine. From the station to the Boulevard des Italiens, a quarter of an hour. There are two hours and a half in hand."

"I shall send one telegram before we start," said Holmes, "to a friend at the Prefecture. A person of this description ought not to sup without an officer upon the stair at the hour when his offer ends. Not before it, madam; you have my word. At midnight."

In the hall the steward, who was strapping a rug, drew the doctor aside with a face of real concern.

"He has not read his Times to-day, monsieur. It lies at the club upon his table, and nobody has cut it. I do not know what becomes of a newspaper which he does not read. It has occurred one time since I am here, and that was for a death."

"Two hours and twenty-five minutes, Holmes," said the doctor, as they went down the steps. "It is a handsome margin. What can possibly go wrong with it?"

"My dear fellow," said Holmes, "when did you last cross the Channel in March?"

The boat train was punctual at Folkestone, and at ten minutes past four the steamer cleared the harbour into a grey and lumpy sea, with a haze upon it which hid the coast of France and a good part of the coast of England. Mr. Fogg stood upon the after-deck with his feet a little apart and his hands behind him, and the doctor noticed that of all the passengers on board he alone had not once put out a hand to the rail.

"It is forty-four years, monsieur," said the steward, who had been looking steadily over the bows since the pier-head. "I quitted France in 'sixty-seven. I have been in Paris one time since, in 'seventy-two, for an hour and twenty minutes, between two stations, in a cab, and it rained without mercy. I did not see one street of my own quarter. I saw an umbrella."

"And Mr. Fogg?"

"He was in the same cab, monsieur. He looked at his watch."

"Then two of the three of us have had eighty minutes of Paris," said the lady, "and the third has had none whatever. I was taught as a girl, Doctor, by an Englishwoman in Bombay, that Paris was the capital of all the vanities, and I have been waiting to see it ever since."

"You are very silent, Holmes," said the doctor. "Do you doubt that the fellow will keep his word?"

"I doubt nothing of the kind. I doubt the sea. Consider the facts, Doctor. A man who has robbed a house by its own punctuality has evidently a theory of the English, and the theory is that we cannot be made to hurry. He has therefore fixed his hour without the smallest fear, and it is probable that he will sit under his clock until the last stroke of it, for the mere pleasure of being right. That is his vanity, and it is our single advantage. It is a curious reflection that we are to recover a jewel by being punctual at a supper. But what is that upon the port bow?"

A quarter of a mile away a brown-sailed fishing lugger lay over at a steep angle, very low in the water, with her mainmast gone by the board and four men clinging along her weather side. It was five minutes to five. The steamer's engines stopped, a boat was swung out, and the second officer, a fresh-faced young man with a whistle, was about to take his place in her when he found a tall old gentleman in a silk hat at his elbow.

"She will not lie as she is lying for five minutes," said Mr. Fogg. "Her mast is over the lee side, and it is beating a hole in her. Bring your boat up under her stern. Do not go alongside."

The young officer stared, looked once more at the lugger, touched his cap without in the least knowing why he did so, and gave the order to his coxswain in those very words. The four men were taken off over the stern. The lugger rolled her side under some four minutes afterwards, and was not seen again.

"You have not forgotten your trade, Mr. Fogg," said the doctor in a low voice.

"It is not forgotten."

The doctor had forty minutes of his own trade in the saloon, where he set a broken forearm upon the dining-table. When he came on deck again the engines were turning, and Holmes stood with his watch in his hand.

"Fifty minutes, Doctor. The Paris train allows the boat a quarter of an hour."

"Fifty-one," said Mr. Fogg.

"You would not have had the captain pass them, Mr. Fogg?"

"No."

The master of the lost vessel, a broad, grey-bearded Boulonnais in a borrowed blanket, had come aft to thank the doctor, and he did it with great dignity, the steward putting it into English one sentence behind him. The lugger had been his father's. Mr. Fogg heard him to the end.

"Ask him the value of the vessel."

"He says nine thousand francs, monsieur, with her nets; and that she was not insured, because the insurance is for people who have nine thousand francs."

Mr. Fogg took out a cheque-book, wrote in it against the lid of a locker, and handed the slip to the fisherman, who turned it over twice in his great hands and looked at the steward.

"He says that a paper is not a boat, monsieur. I have told him that in the house of monsieur it has always been the same thing."

"It will be entered with the sovereigns," said the lady in a low voice to the doctor. "He will find some reason why he ought to have allowed for it."

The fisherman put the cheque inside his jersey, and spoke again, with his eyes upon Holmes's watch.

"He asks, monsieur," said the steward, "why it is that English people who have lost their train are in so great a hurry to be in Paris to-night, and whether it is for a death?"

It wanted eleven minutes of seven by the clock upon the quay at Boulogne when they landed, and the doctor put his watch on to agree with it, as every Englishman does at that place.

"You do not set yours, Mr. Fogg?"

"He has not altered it since 'seventy-two, monsieur," said the steward, "and I have not altered mine since my great-grandfather. It was I who taught him that, though he will not say so. I carried the hour of London round the world in this pocket, and they laughed at me in every port, and at the end it was the watch which was right and the calendar which was wrong."

The Paris express had been gone for six-and-thirty minutes.

"The next train is in Paris at ten minutes past one," said Mr. Fogg, with the red volume under his arm. "There is nothing else in the book."

He walked into the office of the station-master and asked for a special train, and he was heard with the deepest courtesy. A special train could most certainly be had. It could be had at ten o'clock upon the following morning, when the authorisation should have come back from Paris with three signatures.

"In 1872," said Mr. Fogg, "an English company found me one in less than half an hour."

"Monsieur, I do not doubt it. They have no Minister."

"What is the matter with their clocks?" said the doctor to the steward. "The one upon the outer wall says seven, and the one over the platform says five minutes to. Which of them am I to believe?"

"Both, monsieur," said the steward. "In France there are two hours. The clock in the street is for the traveller, and the clock upon the platform is for the train, and the train is always five minutes behind, out of politeness to those who run."

Mr. Fogg, who had come out of the office, did not look at either clock.

Beside the door through which he came there hung a white bill, newly pasted, and headed AVIS AU PUBLIC. Some forty persons went by it, and not one of them stopped. Mr. Fogg, who had read every notice that was set before him since the year 1872, stood with his back to it. The steward bought a newspaper of a boy, the first that he had bought upon French ground for four-and-forty years, and held it for a moment against his coat without opening it.

It was the fisherman who found the way. He had gone into the goods yard, and he returned with his arm about the neck of a small man in a blue blouse.

"He says, monsieur, that the fish of Boulogne does not wait for three signatures. Do you know what is the marée? Every night at twenty minutes to eight the marée goes up to Paris for the markets, and there is nothing in France which passes it; the Calais express is put into a siding to let it by. It is at La Chapelle at a quarter to midnight. This is the guard, who is the brother of his wife, and there is room in the van for those who do not object to herrings. His grandfather told him, monsieur, that in his time the fish went to Paris with horses, at the gallop, and the whole road stood on one side."

"From La Chapelle to the boulevard?" said Mr. Fogg.

"A quarter of an hour, with a horse that is paid."

"Then it is midnight, and there is no margin."

"There is none," said Holmes, "and therefore there must be a second string. While you were being refused a train I was at a garage behind the harbour. There is a racing car of sixty horse-power in it, which ran at Dieppe in the Grand Prix, and a driver who undertakes to be in Paris by midnight if he is not required to be alive upon Saturday. It carries two beside himself. If your fish is stopped by a signal, Mr. Fogg, I shall at least be in that room. I cannot ask for the stone, but I can keep him in talk, for he has a weakness for an audience. It is impossible to say which of us the night will favour, and I conclude that we must try both. You will take the third seat, Mr. Fogg?"

"No. The train."

"Madam," said the doctor earnestly, "a fish van is no place for you. Take my seat in the car."

"I was carried across a part of India upon an elephant, Doctor, though I knew nothing of it at the time, and I was carried out of a fire. I think that I can sit upon a box of herrings. Besides, I am the only one of us who is obliged to arrive, and I prefer to do it with my husband."

At five minutes past seven the great grey car stood throbbing upon the quay, with Holmes beside the driver and the doctor wedged behind them among the spare wheels. Holmes turned in his seat.

"Mr. Fogg! Upon which of us do you put your sovereign?"

The van of the fish train was lit by a single lantern, and it smelt as the hold of a trawler smells. Flat boxes of herring and whiting, packed with broken ice, were stacked along both its sides to the height of a man, and upon three of them, set in a row by the guard and covered with his own coat, the party from Savile Row sat down. Mr. Fogg had the red book upon his knee and his watch in his hand, and he held himself, as the van leaped over the points of Boulogne, precisely as he held himself in the saloon of the Reform Club.

The steward had opened his newspaper at last. He read it aloud, from the first column of the first page, and he omitted nothing, having waited, as he explained, for forty-four years.

"'The price of butter at the Halles.' It is dearer. 'The Seine stands at two metres at the Pont Royal.' Last year, madame, she was in the streets. 'A duel at Neuilly between two deputies; four shots are exchanged without result.' That is as it was. 'The legal hour. The President of the Republic has promulgated the law by which the legal hour of France is the hour of Paris, retarded by nine minutes and twenty-one seconds, and it is in the night of Friday to Saturday, at midnight, that the clocks of the railways, of the posts and of the city will be set back.' Nine minutes! They disputed upon that in the cafés when I was a boy. 'At the Opéra-Comique...'"

Nobody attended to him. Mr. Fogg was working a sum, and the lady had put her bare hand into the nearest box and closed it upon the broken ice.

"That is what it should be," said she. "It is exactly that. What is it that you calculate?"

"The distance run against the time. This train is timed at thirty-eight miles in the hour, and it has kept it."

"And if it should be stopped?"

"Then I shall buy the minutes back. It has been done before."

"With an elephant, as I have been told, and with a ship which you burned under your own feet. What will you burn to-night?"

"Twenty-franc pieces."

Beyond Abbeville, through the door which the guard had left a hand's-breadth open, the lady saw two great lamps standing at a level-crossing gate, and a tall figure upright behind them, which took off its hat.

At Amiens the train stopped under a red light, and it stood there for fourteen minutes while a goods engine was got back upon the rails at the junction ahead.

"Tell the guard," said he to the steward, "that there is a gold piece of twenty francs for the driver, and another for the fireman, for each minute of the fourteen which is recovered before La Chapelle."

The pace thereafter was such that the lantern swung to the roof, and the guard crossed himself at the curve by Longueau.

They went through Creil without a check, and Mr. Fogg closed his book.

"Eight minutes are recovered. La Chapelle at nine minutes to twelve by the clock of the street. The boulevard at six minutes past. We shall be six minutes late."

The newspaper fell from the steward's hands.

"Six minutes! In 'seventy-two it was five, monsieur, and I thought that I should die of it."

"In 'seventy-two you were both of you wrong," said the lady.

"The error was mine. It was a day. This is six minutes, and I have worked it three times."

"Then we shall be six minutes late, and I shall ask him all the same. He may have learned to wait for a lady since he wrote." She was silent while the train roared through a cutting; then she laid her cold hand upon his sleeve. "You have missed your club for a piece of red stone. It is the third time in my knowledge that you have left your road for me, and upon two of them you have been late. Do you find that you regret it?"

The car had neither screen nor hood, and it was driven by a small dark man in goggles, who sang, and who took the villages of Picardy at fifty miles an hour. Beyond Montreuil a farm-cart without a light stood across the whole width of the way, not twenty yards off. The driver did not so much as lift his foot. He put two wheels upon the grass and went between the tail-board and a poplar tree with a few inches upon either side, and the song was not interrupted.

"Is the man mad, Holmes?" cried the doctor, when he had recovered the use of his voice. "And this other, whom we are to meet: you said that you knew him?"

"I met him for a quarter of an hour. He picked my pocket of my watch, Doctor, and he sent it back to me within the day with his compliments. I have never been able to determine which of the two proceedings annoyed me the more."

On the southern edge of Abbeville they were stopped. A gate was shut across the road, a line of rails gleamed beyond it, and a stout woman with a lantern stood before it, who declined with perfect composure a gold piece, an oath, and an appeal to her better feelings.

"It is the marée, monsieur. You might be the President of the Republic, and you would wait for the marée like another."

There came a trembling in the ground, and a long line of dark trucks went by them at the pace of an express, reeking of the sea. The van was the last. Its door stood a little open, and in that slip of yellow light the doctor saw for one second an old gentleman seated bolt upright upon a box, with a watch in his hand, and a small figure at his side which lifted its fingers. Holmes had risen in his place and taken off his hat.

"They are before us, Holmes! How in the world can a load of herrings be before us?"

"They were five-and-thirty minutes behind us at Boulogne. That is a fish worth knowing, Doctor."

It was upon the long descent beyond Beauvais, at a few minutes before eleven, that the off front tyre burst. The car slewed across the road with a scream, ran for forty yards upon the naked rim, and came to rest with its bonnet within a yard of a stone cross. For nineteen minutes by the doctor's watch Sherlock Holmes knelt in the mud of a French ditch in his shirt-sleeves, holding a lamp and passing spanners.

"I have backed the wrong horse, Doctor," said he, as he wiped his hands, "and the reasoning by which I did it was perfectly sound, which is the most instructive part of the matter. I observed that a train may be stopped by one red lamp, and I concluded that a road, which has no signals, must be the safer of the two. It did not occur to me that a road has no time-table either. Mr. Fogg would not have this car, and I perceive now that it was for that very reason. He does not ask which way is the faster. He asks which way can be reckoned. Evidently a fish can be reckoned, and a tyre cannot."

"Then we are beaten?"

"We are certainly late. Whether we are beaten is a question for a lady."

They were stopped a third time at the gate of Paris, by an official of the municipality with a measuring-rod.

"Has monsieur anything to declare?"

"Some petrol, which you may tax by the post, and a doctor of medicine," said Holmes. "Drive on."

Then came the lamps of the great boulevards, and the doctor held his watch to the light as they swung into the last of them.

"It is seven minutes past twelve, Holmes. Is there anything in the world which we can still do?"

The fish train came to its place in the yard of La Chapelle at nine minutes to twelve, and a cab with a white horse was found at the gate, the driver of which was shown a gold piece by the steward and comprehended the whole situation instantly.

"It is not the same," said the steward, with his face at the glass. "Do you see, madame? They have made holes in the ground, with iron flowers over them, and the people go down. That is the Northern station, where it rained. And in that street I was a fireman, but they have taken away the house."

Before the door of the Café Anglais, upon an iron column at the edge of the pavement, stood one of the public clocks of the city, and its two hands were together upon the twelve. The steward observed it as he handed his mistress down, and thought only that the clocks of his own country were not kept as clocks were kept in Savile Row. Mr. Fogg did not look at it. He had his watch open, and he had made the correction which he had made at every glance since Boulogne.

"Six minutes," said he.

A grey-haired head waiter met them at the foot of the stair, and bowed to the lady before she had spoken.

"Madame comes for the gentleman in the Grand Seize. There was an order, madame: a lady was to be shown up at any moment before midnight. I am desolated. Midnight has struck these six minutes; I heard it myself upon the clock of the room, and the gentlemen drank to it. The order is at an end."

"Six minutes, and all for nothing!" groaned the steward. Mr. Fogg closed his watch. The lady stood for some seconds perfectly still, with her eyes upon the newspaper which protruded, very much crumpled, from the pocket of the steward's coat.

"What was it," said she, "that you read to us before Amiens, concerning the hour?"

"It was the butter, madame. It is dearer."

"It was after the butter and the duel. Read it to me again."

He dragged out the sheet and found the place with a shaking finger.

"'The legal hour of France is the hour of Paris, retarded by nine minutes and twenty-one seconds, and it is in the night of Friday to Saturday, at midnight—'"

"That is to-night. Now tell me what your watch says," said the lady to her husband. "Not what you make of it. What it says."

Mr. Fogg opened the case.

"Eleven hours, fifty-seven minutes."

"It is the hour of Greenwich, which you have declined to alter since 'seventy-two. How much is Paris before Greenwich?"

There was a pause which the steward, who had heard only one like it in his service, remembered for the remainder of his life.

"Nine minutes and twenty-one seconds," said Mr. Fogg. "I did not read the notice."

"Nobody read it. He read it aloud, and nobody heard him, himself the least of all. Then it has not been midnight in France at all. It is three minutes to twelve, and the only clocks in Paris which say so are the two that you and he have carried in your pockets from Savile Row." She turned upon the head waiter. "Monsieur, your clock upstairs is not the law of your country. Have the goodness to look through that glass at the clock before your own door, which has not moved since we came, and then to show me up. How long have I?"

"Two minutes and a half."

"Then will you come up with me," said the lady, "or will you stand upon the stair and count them?"

The room which is called the Grand Seize was hung with red and lit with a great many candles. Five gentlemen in evening dress sat at the end of their supper, and the young man of the tailor's window was at the head of the table with his glass in his eye. Upon the cloth before him lay a ruby in a setting of soft gold. A gilt clock upon the mantelpiece gave the time as seven minutes past twelve. He was upon his feet before the door had fully opened, and he bowed.

"Madame! I am in despair. I said that I never waited, and I have waited seven minutes with my eyes upon that door. But the clock—"

"I have come for my stone, monsieur. Your card says until midnight, and it is not midnight. Your Republic decided yesterday that from to-night its hour is the hour which my husband carries. There is the newspaper. It wants two minutes."

He took the sheet from the steward, read the paragraph through his glass, and then, to the stupefaction of his guests, threw back his head and laughed with every appearance of the keenest pleasure.

"Gentlemen, we have drunk to midnight nine minutes too soon. Monsieur Fogg, I set my watch by you for eighteen days, and you were never ten seconds out. I said to myself, here is a house which may be robbed by its own clock, and here is the one man in London who can never come after me, because he must be in a certain chair at a certain minute. I chose your house for that reason, monsieur, as much as for the stone. It was evidently a false theory. You were to be at your club. And you come to Paris—you will permit me—in a fish train?"

"It was the only train," said Mr. Fogg. "One minute."

"And you bring me the hour of my own country, which I, a Frenchman, have not read! Is it possible? I am robbed by the Republic. Well, a sportsman pays."

He took up the ruby from the cloth and laid it in the lady's palm. The door was flung open at the same instant, and Holmes stood in it, hatless, with the doctor at his shoulder and the mud of Beauvais upon his knees.

"Monsieur Holmes! Too late again! No; I ask pardon. It appears that nobody is late to-night."

"Madam," said Holmes, "before you thank him, close your hand."

She closed it.

"It is warm," said the lady.

"Ah, monsieur, you know me! A sportsman pays, madame; but he likes to see first whether his creditor can count her money. I asked you once whether it was not cold to wear, and I did not attend sufficiently to the answer."

"It is a trick of the theatre," said one of the guests, a stout, flushed man with a red ribbon in his coat. "How should a lady tell a ruby from glass with her hand? It is impossible. I will wager fifty louis that it cannot be done."

"Taken, Baron. Shut your eyes and hold out both your hands."

The young man drew a second stone from his waistcoat pocket, and laid the two together in the fat palms. For some seconds the Baron stood blinking. Then his left hand jerked, and his eyes came open.

"Tiens! This one. It is a piece of ice."

"It has been madame's for thirty-eight years. You may send the fifty louis to the fishermen of Boulogne."

He took it from the Baron and gave it to the lady with a second bow, deeper than the first. She shut her fingers upon it.

"It is cold," said she.

"Ten seconds," said Mr. Fogg, and put away his watch.

There was a heavy and regular tread upon the stair. The young man listened to it with his head upon one side.

"And there, to the second, is the only other party in Paris who has read the law. Madame, I have kept my word. Messieurs, I leave you the bill."

When the commissary of police came in, with two agents behind him, he found four bewildered gentlemen, who had met their host at the races, a window standing open upon a side street, and, lying across a visiting-card upon the cloth, a single eye-glass with a yard of black ribbon. The card was addressed to Holmes, and two letters of his name had changed places. Holmes put it in his pocket-book. He then put two fingers into his waistcoat pocket, found his watch there, and turned to the official.

"You were asked to be here at midnight, monsieur. It is my own fault that I did not ask myself by which clock."

"By the clock of the Prefecture, monsieur, which was set back at midnight according to the law," said the commissary stiffly. "By what other clock would you have had me come?"

The clock upon the iron column had begun to go again when they came down into the boulevard, and it said ten minutes past twelve. The steward drew out the great silver watch of his family, held the one against the other, and found that for the first time in four-and-forty years a clock of France agreed with it.

Mr. Fogg had opened the small green book against the column, under the lamp, and the lady read what he wrote there.

Won. Fri. 10 March, 11h 59m 50s p.m.

He looked for some time at the name of the day. By every clock that had been going in Paris ten minutes earlier it had been Saturday when the stone came into her hand, and by the law it was Friday.

"You were wrong once between a Friday and a Saturday," said the lady, "and I am the consequence of it. To-night the whole of France has been wrong between a Friday and a Saturday for nine minutes and twenty-one seconds, and it has given me back my stone. I have been very well served by that error."

"I did not take him," said Holmes. "I arrived, as he was polite enough to observe, in time, and I was of use for the space of one sentence. The case was solved, Doctor, by a lady's hand, by a servant's newspaper, and by a watch which its owner would not alter. It is a singular conclusion to an inquiry, and I must own that it is probably a just one. You may put it among those which I prefer that you should not publish. Mr. Fogg, you were my client. I asked you at Boulogne upon which of us you put your sovereign, and you did not answer me."

"Upon neither. It was upon her." Mr. Fogg turned to his wife. "You asked me a question in the train. No."

"You will not have the man pursued, Holmes?" said the doctor.

"By whom, Doctor? I have no warrant in this country, the lady has her property, and the commissary has an open window. I think that France must catch her own."

"It is ten minutes past twelve by that clock," said the doctor, "we have no rooms, and I am bound to say that three of us smell very strongly of herrings."

"We have a city," said the lady. "Two of you have had eighty minutes of it, and they were wet."

"Madame, my street is twenty minutes from this door," said the steward, "and at the corner of it, in 'sixty-seven, there was a woman who sold fried potatoes until two in the morning."

"Then let us go," said the lady, "and see whether she has kept her hours."
